patient.name: Rajesh Patel

prompts.q: What is a TIA and how is it defined?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the word 'resolved' in the stem is what makes it a TIA.

points.p: Transient neurological dysfunction from focal cerebral ischaemia
points.why: Not a global loss of consciousness.

points.p: Fully resolves, by definition within 24 hours (usually minutes)
Warning sign of impending stroke
points.why: Risk is highest in the first days.

prompts.q: What are the risk factors and the typical presentation of a TIA?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: same risk factors as stroke; examination is normal by the time you see them.

points.p: Risk factors: AF, carotid stenosis, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, smoking
points.why: A carotid bruit is a stem clue.

points.p: Sudden unilateral weakness or speech disturbance that completely resolves
Facial droop, numbness, transient dysarthria
Examination normal at assessment

prompts.q: What are the classic TIA presentations to recognise by name?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one eye = carotid; both eyes, one half-field = posterior.

points.p: Amaurosis fugax: transient monocular visual loss (curtain)
points.why: Carotid atherosclerosis is the usual source.

points.p: PCA territory TIA: transient homonymous hemianopia (occipital cortex)

prompts.q: How do you tell a TIA from its mimics and from stroke?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: negative, sudden, fully resolved = TIA.

points.p: Persisting deficit = completed stroke, not TIA
Hypoglycaemia: check capillary glucose
points.why: The commonest mimic to exclude first.

points.p: Migraine aura: spreading positive symptoms, then headache
Focal seizure: jerking then Todd's paresis

prompts.q: How do you investigate a TIA?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: TIA is clinical; the tests find the cause.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis plus urgent specialist review
Capillary glucose
Urgent carotid Doppler / duplex
points.why: Unless not a candidate for endarterectomy.

points.p: ECG for AF, bloods
MRI with DWI within 24 hours in TIA clinic

prompts.q: What do you do if a TIA patient is anticoagulated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: anticoagulant in the stem changes the pathway.

points.p: Admit immediately
Non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage
points.why: Bleeding can mimic TIA in an anticoagulated patient.

prompts.q: What is the immediate management of a suspected TIA, and what changes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: resolved = aspirin + clinic; ongoing or crescendo = admit.

points.p: Aspirin 300 mg immediately
Specialist review in TIA clinic within 24 hours
Aspirin contraindicated: clopidogrel + PPI
Ongoing symptoms or crescendo TIA: emergency admission

prompts.q: What is the secondary prevention after a TIA, including surgery?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: AF changes the drug; stenosis percentage decides surgery.

points.p: Clopidogrel (dual antiplatelet if high risk)
Atorvastatin 80 mg
BP control, stop smoking
AF: anticoagulate (apixaban/rivaroxaban) instead
Carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic 50–99% stenosis (NASCET); not if occluded

prompts.q: How does a TIA differ from a stroke, and why is carotid disease important?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: infarction is the dividing line.

points.p: Thrombus/embolus transiently occludes, ischaemia resolves before infarction
Carotid atherosclerosis: plaque rupture or thrombus embolises distally
Amaurosis fugax: transient occlusion of ophthalmic / central retinal artery
points.why: First branch of the internal carotid.

points.p: Endarterectomy removes the plaque, reducing embolic risk
points.why: Not done if fully occluded: no flow, no emboli.

glossary.TIA: Transient ischaemic attack: brief focal neurological dysfunction from ischaemia that fully resolves without infarction.
glossary.focal cerebral ischaemia: Reduced blood supply to one area of the brain.
glossary.amaurosis fugax: Painless, temporary, curtain-like loss of vision in one eye from retinal artery ischaemia.
glossary.homonymous hemianopia: Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes, from a lesion behind the chiasm.
glossary.aphasia: Loss of language ability from a brain lesion.
glossary.dysarthria: Slurred speech from weak or uncoordinated speech muscles.
glossary.carotid bruit: A whooshing sound over the carotid from turbulent flow through a stenosis.
glossary.carotid stenosis: Narrowing of the carotid artery, usually by atherosclerosis.
glossary.carotid Doppler: Ultrasound measuring carotid narrowing and blood flow.
glossary.duplex ultrasound: Ultrasound combining images and Doppler flow, used to grade carotid stenosis.
glossary.NASCET: North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial criteria for measuring carotid stenosis percentage.
glossary.carotid endarterectomy: Surgery to remove atherosclerotic plaque from the carotid artery.
glossary.crescendo TIA: Repeated TIAs increasing in frequency, needing emergency admission.
glossary.DWI: Diffusion-weighted MRI, which shows even small acute ischaemic lesions as bright.
glossary.diffusion-weighted imaging: MRI sequence that detects acute ischaemia within minutes.
glossary.TIA clinic: Specialist rapid-access clinic where suspected TIA is assessed within 24 hours.
glossary.atrial fibrillation: Irregularly irregular rhythm that lets clots form in the left atrium and embolise.
glossary.DOAC: Direct oral anticoagulant, such as apixaban or rivaroxaban.
glossary.apixaban: A factor Xa inhibitor DOAC used in AF.
glossary.rivaroxaban: A factor Xa inhibitor DOAC used in AF.
glossary.clopidogrel: Antiplatelet that blocks the P2Y12 ADP receptor; long-term choice after TIA.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor, such as lansoprazole, protecting the stomach.
glossary.lansoprazole: A proton pump inhibitor used for stomach protection.
glossary.dual antiplatelet: Two antiplatelets together (e.g. aspirin plus clopidogrel) for a short time in high-risk patients.
glossary.atorvastatin: High-intensity statin given at 80 mg after TIA or stroke.
glossary.embolus: A clot or plaque fragment carried in the blood that blocks a smaller vessel.
glossary.plaque rupture: Breakdown of an atherosclerotic plaque, exposing material that triggers thrombus.
glossary.ophthalmic artery: First branch of the internal carotid, supplying the eye.
glossary.central retinal artery: Branch of the ophthalmic artery supplying the inner retina.
glossary.infarction: Tissue death from loss of blood supply.
glossary.Todd's paresis: Temporary weakness after a focal seizure that can mimic TIA.
glossary.CBG: Capillary blood glucose, a bedside finger-prick test.
glossary.mimic: A condition that imitates TIA or stroke, such as hypoglycaemia, migraine or seizure.
glossary.internal carotid: The branch of the common carotid that supplies the eye and anterior brain.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man has a 20 minute episode of left arm and face weakness. When seen by his GP 2 hours later, his examination is completely normal. He has hypertension and smokes. His pulse rate is 78 bpm regular and BP 162/94 mmHg. His capillary glucose is 5.9 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis: resolved or not?
Brief focal deficit, fully resolved, vascular risks, mimic excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sudden focal deficit that resolved fully = **TIA**.

elim: No jerking; weakness was a negative symptom.
Glucose is normal.
The deficit has fully resolved.
No spreading positive symptoms or headache.

steps.x: **E. Transient ischaemic attack.** Resolved = TIA; persisting = stroke.

technique.stem: A 64 year old woman is seen in the TIA clinic the day after a 15 minute episode of right-sided weakness that resolved. She takes no anticoagulants. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm regular and BP 148/86 mmHg. Carotid Doppler shows 30% stenosis bilaterally.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate brain imaging?
o: CT angiogram of the circle of Willis

steps.x: Asks for brain imaging in TIA clinic.
Specialist clinic, resolved TIA, not anticoagulated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI with DWI** (NICE, within 24 hours).

elim: For aneurysms or acute vessel occlusion.
No role in TIA.
NICE advises MRI in the TIA clinic when imaging is needed to look for ischaemia or alternatives.
For anticoagulated patients or suspected bleed.

steps.x: **C. MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging.** TIA imaging = MRI DWI; CT only if anticoagulated.

technique.stem: A 69 year old man had a 30 minute episode of slurred speech that has fully resolved. He had a major upper GI bleed from a peptic ulcer last year. His pulse rate is 80 bpm regular and BP 150/88 mmHg. He is not anticoagulated.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial antiplatelet treatment?
o: Clopidogrel with a proton pump inhibitor

steps.x: Antiplatelet choice when aspirin is unsafe.

clues: major upper GI bleed from a peptic ulcer
steps.x: Resolved TIA, aspirin contraindicated by GI bleeding.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clopidogrel + PPI** (e.g. lansoprazole).

elim: Contraindicated given his recent GI bleed.
Not the recommended alternative.
Leaves him at high early stroke risk.
No AF; antiplatelets are indicated.

steps.x: **B. Clopidogrel with a proton pump inhibitor.** Aspirin contraindicated = clopidogrel + PPI.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has sudden painless loss of vision in his right eye, 'like a curtain coming down', lasting 5 minutes. It fully recovers. He has a right carotid bruit. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 158/90 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his visual loss?
o: Embolus from carotid plaque transiently occluding the retinal circulation
Giant cell arteritis of the posterior ciliary arteries

steps.x: Mechanism of amaurosis fugax.

clues: painless loss of vision in his right eye
steps.x: Monocular, curtain, resolved, ipsilateral bruit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Carotid **embolus** briefly blocking the **ophthalmic / central retinal artery**.

elim: Headache, jaw claudication, older, raised ESR.
Gives a bilateral homonymous field defect, not one eye.
Transient obscurations with papilloedema and headache.
Floaters and flashes, not fully recovering.

steps.x: **A. Embolus from carotid plaque transiently occluding the retinal circulation.** Amaurosis fugax = carotid embolus to the retinal circulation.

practice.stem: A 73 year old woman had a 40 minute episode of difficulty finding words and weakness of her right hand this morning. By the time she arrives at the GP surgery, it has completely resolved. She has type 2 diabetes and hypercholesterolaemia. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm regular, BP 158/88 mmHg and capillary glucose 7.1 mmol/L. Neurological examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A sudden focal deficit that fully resolves, with normal examination and glucose, is a TIA.

steps.x: Diagnosis.
Brief, fully resolved focal deficit; glucose normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **TIA** (left carotid territory).

elim: Facial weakness only, and it does not resolve in minutes.
Positive symptoms such as jerking would be expected.
Glucose is 7.1.
The deficit has fully resolved.

steps.x: **E. Transient ischaemic attack.** Resolved focal deficit = TIA.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man has sudden painless loss of vision in his left eye lasting 10 minutes. He describes a black curtain coming down. It fully recovered. He smokes and has hypertension. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 166/94 mmHg. Visual acuity and fundoscopy are now normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Painless curtain-like monocular loss that fully recovers is amaurosis fugax, a carotid-territory TIA.

steps.x: Diagnosis of transient monocular loss.

clues: painless loss of vision in his left eye
steps.x: Monocular, painless, curtain, resolved, vascular risks.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Amaurosis fugax**: a retinal TIA.

elim: Painful red eye with halos.
Persisting loss with 'stormy sunset' fundus.
Headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, raised ESR.
Positive phenomena in both eyes' fields, then headache.

steps.x: **E. Transient ischaemic attack (amaurosis fugax).** Curtain over one eye that resolves = amaurosis fugax.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man had two episodes this week of right arm weakness lasting 10 minutes, each fully resolving. He smokes 30 a day. His pulse rate is 70 bpm regular and BP 160/90 mmHg. ECG shows sinus rhythm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
practice.e: Right-sided symptoms come from the left hemisphere; in a smoker in sinus rhythm the likely source is left carotid stenosis, heard as a bruit.

steps.x: Most likely examination finding.
Recurrent right-sided TIAs, smoker, no AF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Left hemisphere = **left carotid** stenosis: a **left carotid bruit**.

elim: Aortic stenosis; not the TIA mechanism here.
Pulse is regular and ECG is sinus.
Right carotid supplies the right hemisphere, giving LEFT-sided symptoms.
Examination is normal once a TIA has resolved.

steps.x: **C. Left carotid bruit.** Carotid lesion is on the side opposite the limb symptoms.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman had a 30 minute episode of left face and arm weakness that resolved. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 146/84 mmHg. ECG (see item resources). Carotid Doppler shows less than 30% stenosis bilaterally.

visual.title: ECG
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves.

practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her TIA?
practice.e: With AF on the ECG and insignificant carotid disease, the embolic source is the left atrium: cardioembolic TIA.

steps.x: Most likely cause.
AF on the ECG; carotids not significantly narrowed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cardioembolism from AF.**

elim: Young, neck pain, Horner's.
Causes lacunar events; AF is a more convincing source.
Doppler shows less than 30% stenosis.
No systemic features.

steps.x: **A. Cardioembolism from atrial fibrillation.** AF + clean carotids = cardioembolic TIA.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man noticed he could not see things on his left side for 25 minutes. It fully resolved. Visual field testing now is normal. He has hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 156/92 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely site of the transient ischaemia?
practice.e: A transient homonymous hemianopia is a PCA-territory TIA in the occipital cortex opposite the field loss.

steps.x: Site of ischaemia.

clues: could not see things on his left side
steps.x: Transient left-sided field loss in both eyes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Left homonymous field loss = **right occipital cortex** (PCA territory TIA).

elim: Would cause a RIGHT-sided field loss.
Retinal ischaemia affects one eye only.
Causes bitemporal hemianopia, usually from a pituitary mass.
Monocular, not a hemifield in both eyes.

steps.x: **D. Right occipital cortex.** Field defect side is opposite the occipital lesion.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man had three episodes of left arm numbness and weakness in the last 24 hours, each lasting 15 minutes and fully resolving. He is now well with a normal examination. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 170/96 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Multiple TIAs in a short period is crescendo TIA, needing urgent emergency admission rather than routine clinic.

steps.x: Diagnosis of recurrent events.
Repeated resolving TIAs clustering in a day.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Crescendo TIA**: an emergency admission.

elim: Positive symptoms and post-ictal weakness.
A stroke persists.
Spreading positive sensory symptoms then headache.
Not sudden, recurrent and resolving with weakness of a whole arm.

steps.x: **A. Crescendo TIA.** Clustering TIAs = crescendo TIA = admit.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man is seen in the TIA clinic after a resolved episode of right hand weakness and dysphasia. He is fit for surgery. His pulse rate is 76 bpm regular and BP 152/88 mmHg. ECG shows sinus rhythm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to guide further management?
practice.e: All TIA patients who could have endarterectomy need an urgent carotid Doppler.

steps.x: Investigation that changes management.
Carotid territory TIA, surgical candidate, no AF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent carotid Doppler** to look for stenosis needing endarterectomy.

elim: Investigates angina, not TIA.
For seizures.
No role.
Considered later; the carotid is the priority in an anterior circulation TIA.

steps.x: **A. Carotid Doppler ultrasound.** TIA + fit for surgery = carotid Doppler.

practice.stem: An 80 year old woman taking rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation had a 20 minute episode of left arm weakness that has now resolved. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 150/86 mmHg.

Anticoagulated patient with a TIA.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man presents to his GP after an episode of slurred speech 2 hours ago that resolved after 30 minutes. He takes atorvastatin 40 mg. He has no allergies and is not anticoagulated. His pulse rate is 70 bpm regular and BP 154/90 mmHg. Examination is normal.

Resolved TIA, not anticoagulated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aspirin 300 mg now + TIA clinic within 24 hours.**

Far too slow.
Long-term prevention after specialist review.
No AF.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man had a TIA with right arm weakness 3 days ago. Carotid duplex shows 75% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery and 20% on the right. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg. He is fit for surgery.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Carotid endarterectomy of the left internal carotid
Carotid endarterectomy of the right internal carotid
Dual antiplatelets only, repeat duplex in 1 year

clues: 75% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery
steps.x: Symptomatic left carotid stenosis of 75%.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent left carotid endarterectomy.**

elim: The right side does not need treatment.

No AF.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman is seen in the TIA clinic after a resolved episode of left-sided weakness. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. MRI shows no haemorrhage. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 142/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term antithrombotic treatment?
practice.e: If AF is the cause of TIA, anticoagulate (apixaban or rivaroxaban) instead of antiplatelets, once haemorrhage is excluded.

TIA with AF, haemorrhage excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

For non-AF TIA.

practice.stem: A 65 year old man had 15 minutes of left arm weakness that fully resolved. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg. MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging the next day shows no infarct.
practice.q: Which best explains why his symptoms resolved completely?

Resolved symptoms, no infarct on DWI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Transient occlusion; **ischaemia resolved before infarction**.

elim: TIA is ischaemic, not haemorrhagic.
Dead neurones do not regenerate in minutes.
A sudden vascular deficit in a risk-factor patient is organic.
MRI shows no infarct; infarction defines stroke.

steps.x: **B. Ischaemia resolved before infarction occurred.** TIA = ischaemia without infarction.
